at overnatte.explanation: "At overnatte" means to stay the night somewhere, like a hotel, a friend's house or a hostel. "Vi overnatter på hotel" means "We stay the night at a hotel". It is a very useful word when travelling. A place to stay the night is "en overnatning".

sentence.en: We stay the night at a small hotel.

en onkel.explanation: "En onkel" is an uncle, the brother of a parent or the husband of an aunt. Watch the spelling: the "e" drops out before the ending, so it is "onklen" and not "onkelen". Its pair is "en tante" (aunt).

sentence.en: My uncle has a big garden.

en ovn.explanation: "Ovn" is the oven in your kitchen, the one you bake and roast in. Typical phrases are "i ovnen" (in the oven) and "at tænde ovnen" (to turn the oven on). The hob or cooker top is a different word, "en kogeplade".

sentence.en: The cake is in the oven.

forms.da: Er der et offentligt toilet her?
forms.en: Is there a public restroom here?

et offentligt toilet.explanation: "Et offentligt toilet" is a restroom anyone can use, for example in a park, a station or a shopping centre. "Toilet" is an et-word, so the describing word gets a "t" on the end: "offentligt". After "the" it changes to "det offentlige toilet". Some public toilets in Denmark cost a few kroner to use.

sentence.da: Ved banegården er der et **offentligt toilet**.
sentence.en: At the railway station there is a public restroom.

et ord.explanation: "Et ord" is a word. The plural is the same as the singular, so "mange ord" means many words. A dictionary is "en ordbog", which is just "word book". You will use it constantly when learning: "Hvad betyder det ord?" means "What does that word mean?".

sentence.en: I don't know that word.

ofte.explanation: "Ofte" means often. It goes after the verb in a normal sentence: "Jeg går ofte i skoven" (I often walk in the forest). It sits between "altid" (always) and "nogle gange" (sometimes) in strength. If you want to ask how often, you say "hvor ofte?".

sentence.en: We often eat out.

og.explanation: "Og" means and, and it joins words or sentences. The g is usually not pronounced, so it sounds a bit like "o". To say both.. and, use "både.. og". It is also the first word in many fixed pairs, like "op og ned" (up and down).

sentence.en: I like coffee and tea.

også.explanation: "Også" means "also" or "too". It usually goes right after the verb, as in "Jeg kan også lide kaffe" (I also like coffee). When it comes first, it points to the word after it. Be careful with "ikke" (not): "ikke også" is not a way to say "not either"; for that, Danes use "heller ikke".

sentence.da: Jeg vil **også** have en kop kaffe.
sentence.en: I would like a cup of coffee too.

okay.explanation: The same word as English, and Danes use it all the time to agree or show they understand. It is pronounced like in English. It is casual but fine in most situations. For a more Danish option, try "fint" (fine) or "i orden" (all right).

sentence.en: See you at five. – Okay!

oksekød.explanation: "Oksekød" is beef. It is built from "okse" (ox) and "kød" (meat), and it is an et-word. In a Danish shop you will often see "hakket oksekød", minced beef, which is used for meatballs and sauces.

sentence.en: I buy beef at the supermarket.

oktober.explanation: "Oktober" is October. Note that Danish spells it with a k, unlike English. It is written with a small letter and used with "i": "i oktober". In many schools there is a week of autumn break, "efterårsferie", in this month.

sentence.en: There is autumn break in October.

olie.explanation: "Olie" is oil, and it is an en-word. It is used for cooking oil and for other kinds of oil too. For a specific kind you say "olivenolie" (olive oil) or "rapsolie" (rapeseed oil), which is very common in Denmark. In a shop, check the label to see which kind it is.

sentence.en: I fry the meat in oil.

om.explanation: "Om" means about, and also around. It is used for a topic ("en bog om Danmark") and for times ahead: "om en uge" means "in a week". It is also the word for "whether" in sentences like "Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer".

sentence.en: The film starts in an hour.

forms.en: In the evening we watch TV.

om aftenen.explanation: "Om aftenen" means in the evening, as a general habit. It is about what usually happens each evening. Notice that "the" is added to the end of "aften", giving "aftenen". For this evening only, use "i aften".

sentence.en: We eat together in the evening.

forms.en: I am coming in a little while.
See you in a little while.

om lidt.explanation: "Om lidt" means in a little while, soon. It is about the near future, a few minutes or so. It is a gentle way of saying you will do something soon but not right now. For right now, use "lige nu".

sentence.en: The food is ready in a little while.

forms.en: I get up in the morning.
In the morning I drink coffee.

om morgenen.explanation: "Om morgenen" means in the morning, as a regular thing. It describes habits, like what you do every morning. For one particular morning, name the day: "mandag morgen" is Monday morning. The word "the" is added to the end of "morgen".

sentence.en: I go for a run in the morning.

om natten.explanation: "Om natten" means at night, as something that usually happens. It is about the dark hours in general. The "the" is added to the end of "nat", giving "natten". For tonight or last night, use "i nat".

sentence.en: It is quiet here at night.

forms.da: Jeg arbejder fem dage om ugen.
forms.en: I work five days a week.

om ugen.explanation: "Om ugen" means per week or a week, used to say how often something happens. It usually follows a number of times or days: "to gange om ugen" is twice a week. The word "om" works here like "per". It is the same pattern as "om dagen" (a day) and "om måneden" (a month).

sentence.en: I work out three times a week.

omkring.explanation: "Omkring" means "around", and it can be about place or about a rough time or number. "Omkring byen" means around the town, and "omkring klokken otte" means about eight o'clock. It is used a bit like "rundt", but "omkring" is more about being on all sides of something. For going in circles, "rundt" is the more usual word.

sentence.en: We walk around the lake.

ondt.explanation: "Ondt" means pain or hurt and is used in the phrase "at have ondt i" (to have pain in): "Jeg har ondt i maven". "Det gør ondt" means "It hurts". Do not say "Jeg er ondt", because that is wrong. It is related to "ond" (evil), but here it is only about physical pain.

sentence.en: I have a stomachache.

onsdag.explanation: "Onsdag" is Wednesday, and like all day names it starts with a small letter. Use "på onsdag" for the coming Wednesday, and "om onsdagen" for every Wednesday. It is named after the god Odin (Woden), like the English name. Be careful with the spelling, because the "d" in the middle is easy to forget.

sentence.en: The children are off on Wednesday.

op.explanation: "Op" means "up" and shows movement upwards, as in "Kom op!" (Come up!). Danish makes a difference between movement and being in a place: "op" is for going up, while "oppe" means being up there. It is also part of many verbs, like "at stå op" (to get up) and "at vågne op" (to wake up). Its opposite is "ned" (down).

sentence.en: I walk up the stairs.

oppe.explanation: "Oppe" means up there, and it describes where something is, not movement. For moving upward you use "op": "gå op" (go up). "Er du oppe?" can also ask whether someone is out of bed. Think of it as the "staying up" word.

sentence.en: The book is up on the shelf.

optaget.explanation: "Optaget" means busy or occupied. Use it for a phone line, a toilet, a seat or a person who has no time. "Er her optaget?" asks whether a seat is taken. It already ends in "t", so it stays the same for en-words and et-words; the form for more than one is "optagne". The opposite is "ledig" (free, available).

sentence.en: Is this seat taken?

orange.explanation: "Orange" means orange, the colour. It never changes its ending, so it is "en orange bil", "et orange hus" and "orange biler". The fruit is "en appelsin", and the Danes do not use "orange" for the fruit itself.

sentence.en: Her jacket is orange.

os.explanation: "Os" means "us". You use it when something is done to the group you are in, or after words like "med" and "til". When you are the ones doing it, you say "vi". The word is short and sounds a little like "oss".

sentence.en: Do you want to come with us?

ost.explanation: "Ost" means cheese. It is an en-word, so "the cheese" is "osten". Denmark has many cheeses, such as Danbo and Havarti. To talk about one kind, use "en ost", like "en fransk ost" (a French cheese). Cheese on bread is a common lunch.

sentence.da: Jeg kan godt lide **ost** på brød.
sentence.en: I like cheese on bread.

otte.explanation: Means "eight". The "tt" gives a quick sound and the word ends with a soft "e". Eighteen is "atten", which is spelled with an "a" and not an "o". It stays the same before en-words and et-words.

sentence.en: I have eight hours at work.

ottende.explanation: "Ottende" means eighth. It comes from "otte" (eight) and is used for order, floors and dates. It does not change for en-words and et-words, so "den ottende bil" and "det ottende hus" both work. A date like "den ottende marts" is the eighth of March.

sentence.en: He lives on the eighth floor.

ovenpå.explanation: "Ovenpå" means upstairs, on the floor above you. It works both for where something is and for going there: "Jeg bor ovenpå" and "Jeg går ovenpå". The opposite is "nedenunder" (downstairs). It is useful when you talk about houses and flats.

sentence.en: The bedroom is upstairs.

over.explanation: "Over" means over or above, and it is used for position, for crossing and for amounts bigger than something. "Over gaden" can mean across the street. The opposite is "under".

sentence.en: We walk over the bridge.

overalt.explanation: "Overalt" means everywhere. It can go at the end of a sentence or right after the action word. The opposite is "ingen steder" (nowhere), and "et sted" means somewhere. It is a good word to know when you are looking for something.

sentence.en: There is dirt everywhere.

overskyet.explanation: "Overskyet" means overcast, with the whole sky covered by cloud. It is a step stronger than "skyet", which can mean some clouds. It stays the same for en-words and et-words and gets an "-e" for more than one thing. The opposite is "solrig".

sentence.en: The sky is overcast today.
